rows.text: # Animal husbandry — breeds and management ## 1. Introduction Opening frame for **Animal husbandry — breeds and management** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production fill pass. ## 2.…  ·  **Animal husbandry** is the scientific management of livestock — cattle, poultry, fish (pisciculture), bees (apiculture) — for food and products. Modern strategies: improved breeds by **cross-breeding** (e.g. the sunflower-in-chapter example of Karan Swiss cattle), better feed and housing, disease control, and managed fisheries and apiculture.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Trick 1: Branches in one line each: dairy (milk), poultry (eggs/meat), apiculture (bees/honey), pisciculture (fish), sericulture (silk) — five branches with products.  ·  Trick 2: Cattle breeds: exotic high-yield (Jersey, Holstein-Friesian) vs indigenous hardy (Sahiwal, Gir, Red Sindhi); cross-breeding combines both — the two-column answer.

rows.text: **Worked example — why Karan Swiss works in Nepal's climate.** Pure Holstein-Friesian cows give 20+ litres a day in Europe but wilt in South Asian heat and succumb to local diseases. rows.text: ## 8. Summary and self-check 5–10 line chapter summary, self-check questions and the common-confusions list (block VIII) — completed in the unit fill pass.  ·  **Summary.** Animal husbandry raises output per animal through better breeds, feed, housing and health care — with cross-breeding as the central genetic tool and composite fish culture as the ecological one. **Self-check:** can you name the three feeding zones exploited in composite fish culture?
